blocks.x: Okay, it's going. If you want to just state your name and then start off.
Okay, my name is Michael Joseph DeLay.
You might get the spelling too because it's been misspelled.

Michael, M-I-C-H-A-E-L. Michael, Joseph, you know that. And DeLay, capital D-E, capital L-A-Y. Capital L. Capital L-A-Y. I was born in New Orleans, Louisiana. September the 29th, 1909. At 1839, La Hoppe Strait.
Downtown, then, right?
That's in the downtown district, yes.
Can you tell about your parents? Did they play instruments?

My mother was a pianist. She was a very good pianist, but not professionally. She didn't play professionally. And she wanted me to play violin, but I never did like violin. And what made me like trumpet or cornet, as I might say, was Manuel Perez. Manuel Perez's sister, she's the only one that's living today. Her name is Lilia Perez. She's my godmother.
Do you know where she's living about?
Yes, she lives at 1136 Two Row Strait. She's the only one living in the Perez family today.
Is she older or younger than Manuel?

I don't exactly know if she would have been, although Manuel did pass away around 42, 43. I'm not sure what year, but I was somewhere, and I was in the Army, I think it was. Anyhow, and what made me like trumpet or cornet so much is because my mother used to take me there lots of time, visiting when I was a kid. And he was giving lessons, and I just took to the trumpet or cornet. And I always didn't want to play a cornet. So, like I said, she wanted me to play violin, but I didn't like violin. So I went until right after, just right after one, especially, I mean exactly one week rather, after my 16th birthday, I had saved some money. I had a newspaper route, and I used to work in between school vacations. So I just saved that money, and I bought myself a little cornet. It was a little short one. It was a con wonder with a tuning device in the rear. And from then, well, I've started ever since then. And by coincidence, after learning, I learned about six, seven pieces. I hadn't taken any lessons, but I learned about six, seven pieces, and I played a job. That was the carnival day right after that. That was in 1926. It was a dance job or parade? No, it was a parade, in a street parade, on the carnival day. Then I began taking lessons with Manuel Perez. He was my first teacher. Then I sort of got discouraged like kids do, and I put the horn down. I left the horn down for about two and a half to three years. I didn't touch the horn anymore. Then I picked it back up, I'd say around 28 or the latter part of 28. And that's when I started playing. My first job was with Paul Barbaran's youngest brother. He was a drummer. You know, there were three drummers. Lewis, Charles, I can't call his name, the name was the banjo player. We used to call him Fushnik. Everybody around New Orleans knew Fushnik. Well, he left. He went to Chicago years ago. He was a banjo player. And Edgar Saussure was the clarinet, rather the saxophone player. Oh no.
Well, this is Saussure I knew in Chicago, played, Lee Collins played drums. Is that right?
Yeah.
He came from New York.

Well this is Edgar Saussure, he's my wife's first cousin. He's in Frisco today. There must be some relative of that. Undoubtedly he is. But anyhow he played saxophone with us. I don't recall all the guys, but that was, well I would say, my first job after I, when I started over again. Yeah. And meanwhile, I…
Can you tell a little bit about your lessons with Perez? Did he teach you out of the Auburn book or which?

Yes, he did from the Auburn book. But I didn't take too many lessons from him because he left and went to Chicago. Then, so he suggested that I go to Sidney Desveen, had been his pupil previously, maybe, oh I don't know, maybe 10, 12, 15 years previously he had been by his pupil. And in turn he goes out of town. I think it was Chicago if I'm not mistaken.
He was on the boat quite a bit too.
Oh yes. So I had to get another teacher. So I went with old man Shalini.
I never knew him, but I don't think he's living. I've heard a lot of his thoughts about it.
I don't think so. He was very old. He had a trumpet. I mean he had a son rather that played cornet also, a nice cornet player.
Yeah, I've heard people talk about it.

So I went with the old man I think a little over two years. He was living right there on the man in St. Claude, not very far from him. And we used to pay 25 cents for a lesson. 25 cents for a lesson at the time. And that was, well that was up around 29 I imagine. Yeah. And a portion of 30, about 29 anyhow. Yeah that's right. So I got a job at Tucky Hall on the last of 29. That was my first regular job. That was the fine dance hall. I took a band in there. We worked about two and a half years over there.
I remember I was there when Kid Nene was playing, we were on the play there on Lincoln Park.

Yeah he played there on Lincoln Park. I met him later in later years I went back and worked there when it was Budweiser then. You see I went there and worked later on. I think around 37 or something. With Butler Rap, he had the band over there at the time. That was around 37.
Did you ever play any other instruments when you were a kid even before you took up cornet, like guitar, fool around with them?

No, the only thing I did fool around with as a kid was piano. I fooled around with it. To be honest I never did turn out to really be a pianist. I know the Kord Foundation, I'm not much on the article. Your mother had a piano in there at home I guess. I just sort of picked it up that way a little around there because that was about the first thing. But incidentally though, I was given a banjo by a guy. The guy just gave a banjo, but I didn't even know the guy. I mean it was a big surprise. I did start on that banjo before I started on the cornet. What made me learn the banjo was because a friend of mine, Sidney Cates, he was taking it up at the time. I was watching him and everything else about the lessons and everything. And I just caught on to it and I like it pretty well and I did pretty well on it. Then that's where my heart came along. Although I didn't, but I mean I didn't have too much interest in it, no more than fool around. Then fool around ukulele, I used to play ukulele a lot around there.
Do you remember any of the parades or any other early bands or dance artisers when you were a kid?

Oh yes, in fact I remember practically, I should remember all of them because my aunt, her name, it's Kalis Dele, she was my father's oldest sister. She gave dances continuously. Oh, where did they give those dances? She used to give at the economy hall, at the cooperatives hall, the Jeanne Zami and the Franz Zami. She gave them many dances. Most of the old timers remember, but in those days, well I was a kid, although interested in music. Did you hear the music? Did you hear the dances too? Yes, yes, yes. You got to go there. Yes, you know we couldn't naturally dance or anything, but we were there. They took us to everything. So, Maria Perez used to play for us sometime. And in fact she had Kit René a lot, she had Punch, had Buddy Pt, to play for a different time. In fact I used to go give the guys, I mean not give, but I mean she used to send me to give me a receipt and I'd bring it to her. Of course she used to send me all over when I was a kid, you know, and I was always interested in music.
Mother's dances, and they weren't the organization, they gave it just the private party.

Well, this particular thing that I'm talking about, it was my aunt that gave the dance herself, you see. That's how I come to, you know, be really interested. I remember, I'll tell you another thing, I remember when a lot of bands they used to be playing, they was going to the, you know the economy hall? The very street hall used to turn, we used to live right next to where the San Jacinto is, that great big brown house.
Well John Slaseby said something you told him that you were there when they built San Jacinto?

Oh yes, I was living right next door. In San Jacinto it was a big, it was a, you could see it had been a fine home, the house, there was some German people, I don't recall their last name, but I know the boy's name, he was around my age, I mean the boy was around my age, his name was Norman. He had an older sister by the name of Yvonne, very very pretty girl and my mama named my sister after her, named my baby sister Yvonne, right after her. And my baby sister was born in 15 and I remember that well.
Oh by the way, I keep changing the subject, do you have any brothers or anything?
No brothers, I have two sisters. Two sisters. I am the oldest. I have a sister, a few years younger than, I think about six or seven years younger. It's just three of us all together, that's all.
Well go ahead about this hall, what year did you build that about?
Oh this, I don't recall, I really don't recall what year it was built.
Let's see, you were born in 1909? I'm born in 1909.

Nine. I don't recall, I know when the San Jose Center they bought the building and they had their… Before 1920 then I guess. I don't really recall, I really don't recall, but I know they bought the building and later years there the building was knocked down and they built their club and everything. I did remember that.
Still they have dances there sometimes. They do huh?
On Sunday nights. Oh yeah, that's September so in 1929, I mean in 1915, that was my birthday, I was six years old that day.
I remember that very well.

Boy I remember a lot of incidents of when I was riding a bike up and down the house, my grandmother slapped me, you know some old people that took the bike and put it in there, and they were kneeling praying. But you know we didn't have sense enough to know any danger. It was a heck of a stone because I remember the mailman passing the tomate antibody.
I was going to ask about the early parades, the ones that if you remember what the bands were like.

Well in the parades, well I remember, well I know, I tell you one thing, the favorite one, one of the main favorites of the kids was Lewis Armstrong. Because all they had to say, oh yes, here come Lewis Armstrong and all the kids just tear out the house. Oh yes, everybody used to tear, you know, you know second line of the halls, I know you know about that. Oh yeah, I remember that. And gosh, and they were loaded I think. But I mean, the music always did touch me, no kidding, I mean, I just like it and always, and he was one of our favorites. Well naturally, Manuel was really one of my favorites too. To be honest, Manuel was my first favorite in later years, then Lewis Armstrong was my favorite. But Manuel was my first favorite, knowing him first and everything too. Then we had Kid Shots, if you recall, Kid Shots. There were some records of him, right? And I was created by Punch and Kid René, and Celestan, Papa Celestan, I worked with him in later years. I never dreamed that I'd work with him in later years, but I worked with him. Well there was all that was favorites around there, you know, and Buddy Pt, they went for Buddy Pt.
Can you tell more about his style? Because John said Buddy Pt, that you play like him sometimes, you play a little chorus and

all that. Buddy Pt, well, what I would say was a lot of, in those days they used to call it runs, we call them chords nowadays, you know, breaking chords, you know what I mean? Because you get to, in later years we studied those things and we actually properly, in other words, probably naturally knew what we were doing. You would put it that way, you understand what I mean? So I just, I had an idea, I always wanted to play on that type, just a lot of execution. And even before, even before I knew, I knew too much, any amount about music, I was playing a lot of horn. Because I practiced that way. Practiced to see how fast I could play, how many notes I could make. Not say exactly, count, but a lot of articulation, you know. And I just learned how to play that way. But, but one of the main things, I mean, I was falling behind Lerse Armstrong, I didn't tell you about this. No. Until 1930, Professor, an old violin player, Robichaud, he was living upstairs over this dance hall and he came down one night, you know.
Which dance hall was it?
Over the fire dance hall. Over the fire, he did there, what?
He lived there, upstairs.

And he worked at the Lyric Theater right next door. Yes, right next door. Well, of course, in the days when I'm talking about the Lyric Theater that burned down, it was a parking ground, I'm talking about 1930. So he came down one day, he called me, he talked, he said, son you play nice. He said, but you shouldn't copy behind people so much. He said, although it does sound good, he said, but it just boosts the other person. He said, although I like Lerse, he said, but it's best to try to get your own style. And this guy as a saxophone player came through. In fact that touched me what he told me. And I thought about it too. Following your chick and you're trying to play note for note behind a guy and everything. Although the people went for it, but I mean you wouldn't go too far in the hometown with that, because they ate it up, they liked that, you know. But anyhow the people, I mean what I want to say, what made me change, I thought it changed a little style. Maybe I may have a little effect of it like Lerse. I imagine I have some passages I imagine. Almost everybody is influenced by Lerse. You always see, yes because practically everybody, just like you said, has been influenced by Lerse. Not only trumpet players, practically everybody.
Yeah, singers even.

So one guy gave me a, I don't know, made me feel changed sort of. I took to this guy, his name was Gene Porter, a saxophone player. Oh, yeah. He had just got out of Des Dune's band. Des Dune had died and he came from, I think he died in Mexico and they came over there and there was a guy by the name of Greg, played trumpet, and this little guy, Henry Halloway, his name is Kildee we call him, I think he's around New Orleans yet. Well they all came over there, oh a lot of musicians, they came over there just to get a workout at the dance hall. And I was amazed by the, about this guy not knowing numbers and having the guys to call the chords. And I talked to him and he told me about it and I just went and flew with the piano, I knew the chords, at least that's the only thing I didn't know was the foundation, not articulation, I never was much. And I followed it from there and I began playing what you call a chord system. And incidentally, hate to put it that way, but I think I was about the first trumpet player to actually start to play a chord system around New Orleans. Actually knowing that I mean.
Yeah knowing what chord you were playing.

Knowing what you were doing. I don't mean to say a lot of variation because so many trumpet players before and older and probably before I was born did a lot, whereas I've heard on later in later years. But I mean actually following that chord pattern, I just, I could just start, and the average guy around New Orleans knows me around my, say around my age or maybe a little older. They know, they tell you that. Like Eddie Pearson and all these guys, you know Eddie Pearson. Because I worked with Pierron, you know, I worked with Pierron about two years. You know what I mean?
Where did you work with him?
On the boat. On the boat. On the boat. Which boat was it? The Gavaloa? No, it was the president.
Well the president is there now, it's still there.

And then Pierron gave it up and I think he went into his other little business or something and Paul Barberant took the band over. And I worked with Paul Barberant I'd say about two years or so, maybe more. But anyway I worked with Paul Barberant until I went right in the Army. That was in 41 in April. And then he was the last band that I worked with in New Orleans. And I went in the Army and stayed four years and a half and went home to see my people, my mother and father. And I came right, I said that three weeks. I worked with Handel incidentally on piano when I was there. John Handel, Seitz-Fort Blanc, yes. They say very good. Oh yes. Well I worked with him on piano because Joe Robinson was sick or had his tonsils out or something. And he know what to expect of me on piano, you know what I mean. It was more accompanying, which I know the accompaniment because most everything I know on my horn I know on the banjo and the piano. I know the chords. I have that pattern that I understand. But otherwise he couldn't expect no solo or anything because I never was much on the piano. Not in, like I said, articulation or I couldn't do anything.
Well I think I've wrote kind of a horn in the years now. When did you change over the trumpet?

Oh when I changed over the trumpet, my first trumpet I bought was a busher. I bought that busher in 30. But I didn't like it because it was very keen and very, very long and not knowing better in those days. I didn't know that I wasn't getting, it didn't have, it didn't carry much volume. And incidentally somebody stole it. And I don't think I bought it very much. And I went right back to a con, which I had had a con trumpet, a cornet when I started, and I had a con trumpet. Practically wore that one out and I bought another con trumpet. Then I went to a marten, a marten trumpet. That one was lost right here. Yeah I left that one on the sidewalk. I had just come from playing in Downey. We had played all sorts of little circus type deal like deal. And I lost, I left it on the sidewalk, helping the guy with his drum. Then I turned around and I liked the marten so well I got another marten. And said that I have this marten yet, and I say this marten is 11 years old. And although it's practically worn, the Pistons is worn, I still like it. At present, I tell you what I do, I have five horns at present right now. Oh yes. Oh yes. Oh yes. I have a, I said that I have a busher with such a, such a bargain with a practically give away. It's a brand new horn, the guy gave it to me for $50. His son didn't want to do anything with it. But this little busher, this is a good busher. And I have that one. And I have a good King Cornet right now. Then I have another little cornet, a couture, a little French, but it's practically worn. And I have another little cornet made by Lion and Healy, which is practically worn too. That's all I said.
And you know there's a little old short marten?
Yeah, a little cornet. Yeah, a little cornet. Yeah, a little short cornet.
I mean like they used to play in Emanuel Perez and all those guys. A little tiny short marten. Yes, yes.

Yes, I only say the King is larger. The King, the King is, it's a cornet but it's larger. It's almost like a trumpet. It's a beautiful thing. But I can't seem to do so well with it because I can't, I don't have a mouthpiece that, I have about eight or ten but I'm tired buying mouthpieces, I'm giving my money away. And I'll probably get rid of it, you know, because I mean I can't wait for mouthpieces.
No, you have to have a shank to-

But otherwise I like it, it has such good volume, you know. So I still use my old marten and I'm using this busher, I use the both of them. I seem to get just as much out of those marten as the snow work.
You say you play bass and violin.

Oh yes, well bass, oh well incidentally I want to tell you this, my first job on bass violin, Ernie Canguletta gave me that job. I was tickled pink, I guess I would have played for nothing. Because you know I was so tickled. My little buddy, we played at Delpit's I think it was, I don't know if the place is operating yet, that was in Uptown Station, like around, oh I don't know exactly, a couple of the basses above the new bass and canal. Kaliop I think. Oh yeah. Kaliop and Franklin was it?
Might be, yeah.

I think it was Kaliop and Franklin, well that's the first job I ever played on bass. And then I like bass. Now I've played the most, I've worked with Johnny Sincere on bass too. You know a couple of little parties like that? He came down and I was delivering, I mean I was delivering, I was running cab then. I worked with Johnny and Tats, you know Adolph Alexander? Oh yes, yeah. Well I flew around with them and worked on bass then. I didn't do too much on bass because I was really busy mostly on my horn most of the time. Now since I've been here I've worked on bass a lot. I've worked with a guy called Jonas Hodge, I don't know if you know him. He's, well he's from Minden, Louisiana and I happened to be his sergeant when we were in the Army together. And I worked with him on bass. I worked with him maybe about seven or eight months. That was during the time I was delivering mail. Well he was going out of town, as long as he didn't go too far I went with him, you know. Then I stopped and I played other jobs on bass around here. A pretty good bit anyhow, you know. Because bass financially speaking when you're not working regularly I have a better house financially with it. I do better. Oh yes I do better with it. But otherwise I always still want to play my horn so I see. When I joined this little club, you know this little Southern California Hot Jazz Society, a lot of those senior guys playing Dixieland. But to be honest I never, I had never known too much about Dixieland to play it. But I could always sort of keep some of those numbers in my mind. And some of those, no kidding, because Big One had picked it up, I practically knew them. A lot of numbers the guy asked me, you know this number? I said no. And they'd probably pick it up or something, then I turned around and said yes. It's because I didn't know them by name. Now I don't say I knew all of them, Bill. But gosh, I mean it didn't take me no time to play them because I've heard them, it seemed to be instilled in you. Why haven't you heard about them? You heard them at all the dances when you were a kid, when I was a kid. And being so, you know, liking music so much I guess that's why it didn't take me long to run them. I think I played practically the majority of the Dixieland, but I know, and then Joe, Joe Dazberg, he has a book with them too. When did you join Joe? I did, I joined Joe and I just joined Joe about, I'd say 15 months ago, about 15 months ago. We had about eight, nine months steady work between a couple of jobs like that, you know. Although he's not doing anything now, you know. That's the reason why I have this little outfit now, you know.

Yeah. I was going to ask some more about those dances, say at Franz and Me, which was sort of one of the society places I understand. Yes. And what type of music did they play? Would they have played much Dixieland there or did they play mostly like quadrilles or waltzes?

Well to be honest, I wouldn't say that I really remembered exactly what type of music, but it seemed to be the same sort of New Orleans blend type music. To be honest, to say that, to remember exactly what they played, I wouldn't, I couldn't say that I remember, you know, exactly what they played.
Or do you remember anything about those dances that you're at? Oh yeah, yes. That is that they have dinner sometimes, some people told me around midnight they'd stop and eat dinner.

Well, no I tell you what, I remember how she used to do it. She used to go there with big tubs full of sandwiches, well wrapped, very well made with my grandmother probably did help and my grandmother and my mother, they met all the ladies around the house, they helped fix them up and very neat and nice, chicken sandwich, different things, a nice good punch and ice cream, that's all, that's what they had over there. I remember around twelve o'clock, they used to make them play this, it was the Gettysburg March. Oh yeah, six eight March. And the people were so used to it, everybody knew what to do and they'd march and they'd form maybe single and double and then quadruple and so forth and they'd march, I did remember that and then they'd do it in an orderly manner and then they'd pass as they would and they'd get sandwiches and so forth and after it was, everybody had a sandwich or whatever they had to get then the band stopped and they went and ate. Because I remember the band was playing upstairs at the time, I think on the, we used to call them galleries in those days, you know, we call it, over here around here they call it poach I think, they used to call it a poach you know. And the artesian hall too, incidentally, that little artesian hall. She gave dancers over there too and I remember they had to play upstairs there too, particularly. I have some pictures of that. Oh yes, the artesian hall. Well practically, I remember, most all the halls I would say in the Tremé anyhow, you know, in that part of the town she gave that, she didn't give any dancers uptown. Because in other words, majority, I'd not say majority, all the dancers she gave there was strictly invitational. It was people you knew, and if it was 400 people, you could almost count on the whole 400 people being there. Everything was paid for before, before the dance was, you know, everything was paid for already. Yeah, I understand. It was a couple of this and that. And before, I mean, I imagine two, three weeks before the dance went on, everything was paid for, was taken care of because the people brought them out. I remember we used to come and knock on the door and bring the money. You know, people didn't travel much in cars. Too many people didn't have cars in those days. Not the poor people, no, not around that way. And they'd come over there on the street, they'd bring you the money. And before you know it, she'd probably have all the money. It's all, like I said, everything was figured out, the profit and everything, and they're just going with the dance. Oh, what I was getting ready to tell you, Bill, what I used to like is when I used to sit on a step on Domain and Veri, I'd sit down there, and even, the only thing I am really good on, I was with spelling. And I used to spell everything, and I'd say, V-I-L-L-U-R-E, the various streetcars, and I could, but they used to tell, I used to tell them from when they hit Ramport Street, and I'm at Domain and Veri, but they thought that I could read the letters. It's not that I could read the letters, they were in different colors. The broad streetcars had the blue, City Park had the green, and Veri had the brown, so you could see the color at least from Veri to Ramport. And they thought it was amazing, they thought I could read those things. But what I want to say, then the bands, a lot of bands used to be playing on the streetcars, going to work, you know. The whole band, it's set up right in the streetcars, that very streetcars. Oh, many, lots of occasions we'd hear the bands and we didn't know what it was coming from.
The bands would be playing on the streetcars.

On the streetcars, oh yes, I've heard that many times. On the streetcars. Now, to say what band it was, I wouldn't know. But we know that they were going to Ursula, and there were two more blocks from Domain, and they were getting off there. They'd just sit up and just play, you know. Things that you would hardly think of doing nowadays, or they wouldn't do it because things are too congested, the way things are nowadays and everything. Because, you know, a guy, I think he had a little fifty cents per minute, a dollar permit to carry his bass violin. Now I understand, I don't think a guy can get on a bass, on a car. You hardly have any cars there except at St. Charles and Canal.
I've been asked about some of the trumpet players. Do you remember Sam Morgan's band?

Sam Morgan, yes, Sam Morgan. I remember Sam Morgan very well. And I remember, just trumpet players? I remember Lee Collins. Oh, yeah. Oh, he was one of my favorites. I'd say in later years, right after I began playing, he was really one of my favorites. You know, of course, Lewis Armstrong on top all the time. I guess anybody else in those days felt the same. But Lee Collins was really one of my favorites. I'd say like in the years, beginning around 30. And even in 29, I was a short pass. No, no, it was before 29. I'm talking wrong now when I was a short pass. But I was a big barber. Kids didn't have long pants like they do start off with long pants. And I was too big for my age and I just wanted long pants. I used to put them on just to go around the tuxedo garden. Oh, yeah. Just to hear this guy, Lee Collins. And the main thing I used to like to hear him, after he played that number I'd probably go, Ain't she sweet? You remember that? Oh, yeah. You know, you remember those things like that. Guys, especially the guys that you-
Is that the Astoria Hotel, that place?

That place where I'm talking about? No, it was a tuxedo. This was on Franklin and Bienville. Old man at a grass shelf. Oh, yeah, sure. He owned the place, if you recall. In the district. In the district.
In the district.

In the later years he owned two blocks from there, the Rampart and Bienville, the doghouse. I worked for him. Oh, yeah. I worked for him with Artiz. Without Artiz Crosby? I worked for him later years over there. He's the paddock farm. Oh, is that right?
Mm-hmm.
Is that the paddock? No, I mean he's not the emergency.
Oh, he's at the paddock. Oh, he's at the paddock.
Oh, yeah.
In Crosby's.
Well, that was-
With Bill Matthews' band.

But I kept working, no kidding, I kept working. That's why I never could really get to that base much, not around New Orleans. Never could get to the base too much around New Orleans. Yeah. I kept working all the time. We could all leave one job and go around there. And then you could pick jobs, you could get angry and maybe quit and go in another job, but you can't do that nowadays. You don't do those things out there. You don't quit jobs. Put it around.

Well, before our tape runs out, we're in a couple minutes of the street. Is there anything else you can remember about Manuel Perez's lessons, how he taught to me and I feel he's very strict? Did he ever get his horn out to play with you or what did he do?
Well, I really didn't go by Manuel too much, but he did take his horn out a couple of times. The only thing that was sort of embarrassing for me was Manuel tried to get me to sing my notes first.
Oh, yeah.

That's what I wanted to say. I heard he did that. And for us singing, I can't sing a bit. And actually, to me, it was very embarrassing because I'm a sort of self-conscious person. In fact, up until today, I'm still self-conscious. The only time when you see me do something freely is because within myself I know I can do it. Yeah. Or I think I can. If I don't, I don't have the guts. I just don't have just ordinary guts on it. That's my trouble. I don't have too much guts and I know I can't sing. And it was sort of embarrassing for me, which I found out later years, I always did say after that I think that is the best way to learn. Away from it. But he tried, he wanted to teach me without the horn. But he said, since I want the food with the horn, he let me go. He said, but that was best. And after all these years I found out it's best if you learn the music without any instrument whatsoever, then turn around and learn the end. But you know kids are, you know, at 16 years old, you want to get that horn. Now see all the kids are the same, which I'm not saying it's right, but all kids are the same.
That's what they want.
They go get the horn and they want to play the horn. You see? But like I said, in later years I found out that's the best method in the world. If a person only has enough.
Your other teachers especially, what's his name, how do you pronounce it? Shalini?
Shalini. I always wondered how to spell it. I never did see it spelled. I've seen it spelled.
I'm not sure how to spell it. We can look it up some place. How did he teach? Do you remember? He taught all instruments, didn't he?
I don't exactly know if he did. But most of all, I know who was going over there. Do you know Lionel Ferbis? No. Lionel Ferbis, he said no.
No, I don't think of him.

Lionel Ferbaud, his name is sort of pronounced in the French pronunciation. Well you find out about him when you go in. You ask him, he's going to laugh like heck when you tell him about it. He and I went to lessons together. And well, Lionel was never a little guy that think very much. In fact, I don't know if he ever learned, but he's a wonderful musician. He tried to be, and he suffered with asthma all his life. He and my little cousin Lionel, I think they used to, Lionel Curran, he didn't play music, but they used to go to the hospital together I think. You'd meet one another and suffer with asthma. It's a funny thing that he could really play the horn, you know what I mean? And you know they used to coax me into playing a number for them. And I'd play an old man, say I know that's that dawn delay, you know, he'd be about to beat about the only ones. I'd put my horn in the music just to play a number. They'd ask me to play. Some of them had just started, some of them didn't play at all. And you know I just wanted to play. I was, in fact I stood way ahead of myself, you know. I'm way ahead of the music anyhow. I mean, not that it was doing you any good, because musically it doesn't do you any good to get ahead of yourself on the instrument. The idea I got more of the instrument before I got the music, you know, I put it that way. You understand?
Yeah. You used to fake a good deal more than you started.

Oh yes. Well, that was practically the trend around there. If I listened to the guys, if you listened to the guys, you wouldn't even want to listen. Yeah, that's right. If you listened to the older guys, the majority of the old guys, you wouldn't hardly want to listen even. No kidding. Because if it don't be familiar, I don't guess I'd ever want to listen. Not in that era, because they were music conscious, which nowadays the guys, the youngsters, they have a better advantage of that. They don't do that anymore. Yeah. The majority of the kids, they want to learn the proper way, and in fact, most everybody goes out to learn the proper way. But in those days, there were so many of them, they didn't fool around with any music at all. So they just figured since they was planning on making money and wasn't planning or didn't know anything about music, they just thought it was all right. They take it for granted that way, you see. But later years, people began moving and moving around, meeting different companies and everything like that, you see.
Was there any other trumpet player you liked in addition to Louie, Emmanuel, and Lee Collins? Did you hear Chris Kelly much?

Oh, Chris Kelly, yes. Well, I just forgot the name of Bill. In those days I practically, I knew every guy, I knew every guy in those days that was playing and everything. And Bunk, oh, Bunk, you know, Bunk here, stop and he'd start over and he'd stop and he'd start over. But I knew Bunk and everything. I met him lots of time. I knew Iberia when I was working with Paul. Oh, you'd known him over there? Yes, I used to go with Isaiah Morgan, Ike Morgan, Sam Morgan's brother. Well, I played with him a lot, you know. We used to go all around the little Mississippi towns. He had a big name around there.
How did Bunk sound in those days in New Iberia?

Oh, Bunk sound nice. Oh, yeah, Bunk sound nice. Because I only knew him in the same place. That's how many years ago, you know, although I'm not around that equal in age, but what I mean, that's way back. Way back enough for him to at least, might be. Mm-hmm .

segments.title: Opening, name and birth in downtown New Orleans
segments.summary: DeLay gives his name and spelling and says he was born in New Orleans on September 29, 1909, in the downtown district.

segments.title: His pianist mother and godmother Lilia Perez, sister of Manuel Perez
segments.summary: His mother was a non-professional pianist who wanted him to play violin. Manuel Perez's sister Lilia, his godmother, is the last living Perez.

segments.title: Buying a cornet at 16, first parade, and first jobs after the break
segments.summary: Visits to Manuel Perez's lessons made him want cornet. He bought one at 16, played a 1926 carnival parade, quit for about three years, then in 1928 took a first job with a Barbarin brother's band.

segments.title: Lessons with Manuel Perez from the Auburn book
segments.summary: He had few lessons with Perez, who left for Chicago and sent him to Sidney Desvigne.

segments.title: Studying with old man Shalini and the Tuxedo Hall job
segments.summary: Lessons with Shalini cost 25 cents for over two years, to about 1929. He then got his first regular job at a dance hall, later working Lincoln Park again in 1937.

segments.title: Other instruments as a kid: piano, banjo, ukulele
segments.summary: He fooled around on piano, was given a banjo and learned it before cornet, and played ukulele.

segments.title: His aunt's dances and early bands in Tremé
segments.summary: His father's oldest sister gave dances at Economy Hall and other halls, hiring Manuel Perez, Kid Rena and Punch. As a boy he ran errands for her.

segments.title: The house beside San Jacinto Hall and his sisters
segments.summary: He grew up next to the building that became San Jacinto Hall, remembering the neighbours' children. He says he has two younger sisters and no brothers.

segments.title: Boyhood favourites in the parades: Armstrong, Perez, Kid Shots, Celestin
segments.summary: Kids loved the parade bands. His favourites were Manuel Perez first, then Armstrong, plus Kid Shots, Punch, Kid Rena, Celestin and Buddy Petit.

segments.title: Playing like Buddy Petit and Armstrong; Robichaux's advice to find his own style
segments.summary: He played fast runs and followed Armstrong note for note until old violinist Robichaux told him in 1930 to develop his own style.

segments.title: Learning the chord system from Gene Porter
segments.summary: Saxophonist Gene Porter, newly out of Des Dunes' band, showed him to call chords by number. DeLay says he was among the first New Orleans trumpeters to play by chord system.

segments.title: Working on the SS President with Pierson and Paul Barbarin until the Army
segments.summary: He worked about two years on the boat under Eddie Pierson, then with Paul Barbarin until entering the Army in April 1941. He also once filled in on piano for John Handy.

segments.title: His trumpets and cornets over the years
segments.summary: He lists the Buescher, Conn and Martin horns he bought, lost or had stolen, and the five he owns now, including a King cornet.

segments.title: Playing bass: first job, Delpit's, and later bass work in California
segments.summary: His first bass job came from Ernie Cagnolatti. Later he played bass with Johnny Sincere, Adolphe Alexander and an Army friend, and with Joe's Dixieland group in the Southern California Hot Jazz Society.

segments.title: Society dances in Tremé: food, the Gettysburg March, bands on streetcars
segments.summary: He recalls his aunt's invitation-only dances, the midnight sandwiches and march, and bands playing on streetcars going to work.

segments.title: Sam Morgan and hearing Lee Collins at the Tuxedo
segments.summary: He remembers Sam Morgan's band and Lee Collins as a favourite, whom he went to hear in long pants at the Tuxedo on Franklin and Bienville.

segments.title: Working for the Tuxedo owner at the Doghouse, with Crosby and Bill Matthews
segments.summary: He worked later for the club owner at the Doghouse and Paddock. He says there was always plenty of work in New Orleans, and musicians could quit and pick jobs.

segments.title: Perez had him sing his notes first
segments.summary: Perez made him sing notes before playing, which embarrassed him. He later decided learning music apart from the instrument is the best method.

segments.title: How Shalini taught, and fellow student Lionel Ferbos
segments.summary: He cannot say how Shalini taught. He recalls going to lessons with Lionel Ferbos, who had asthma, and getting ahead of the music on his horn.

segments.title: Faking versus reading in the old days
segments.summary: He says older players mostly faked, whereas younger musicians now learn properly.

segments.title: Chris Kelly, Bunk Johnson and playing with Ike Morgan in Mississippi towns
segments.summary: Asked about other trumpeters, he says he knew Chris Kelly and Bunk Johnson, whom he met in Iberia, and played with Sam Morgan's brother Isaiah around small Mississippi towns.
